headline: Anthropic Valued at $900B for Having Competent Chatbot Competitors
subheadline: The startup has discovered a revolutionary pricing strategy: charge based on what OpenAI's board meetings probably cost.
source_headline: Sources: Anthropic could raise a new $50B round at a valuation of $900B
body_html:
Anthropic, the maker of Claude, has received multiple preemptive offers valuing the company between $850 billion and $900 billion. This is what happens when 'competitive product' and 'someone else raised money at a high valuation' become investment theses. The startup appears to have cracked the code: if your competitor exists and is well-funded, you too can be worth nearly a trillion dollars. No revenue targets required.

To contextualize this pricing miracle, Anthropic reached a $900 billion valuation faster than most Fortune 500 companies reach operating profitability. The company has achieved this feat by doing something genuinely difficult—building a large language model—and then pricing itself as though it had solved scarcity itself. The preemptive offer structure suggests that investors are competing to pay inflated prices before other investors get the chance, which is either peak FOMO or peak asset price disconnection. Possibly both.

The term 'preemptive offers' deserves special mention here. In normal industries, this means you're so valuable that buyers will move fast before you shop around. In 2024+ venture, it means everyone is terrified of missing the narrative and will bid anything to stay in the game. Anthropic has simply turned 'someone else is investing in AI' into a $50 billion fundraising event.

By next quarter, expect the follow-on announcement: Anthropic raises $75B at a $1.2T valuation, citing 'strong market validation and investor momentum.' Which is finance-speak for 'we printed a press release and people didn't say no.'
glossary_definition: A bid made without seeing the actual product's unit economics, deployed solely to ensure you don't miss out on whatever everyone else is doing.
